citations.narrative:
The outdoor housing facilities for the otters and the red foxes had areas in need of repair. A metal drainage cover in the
otter enclosure had portions that had broken off creating large openings that posed an entrapment risk. The portion of the
enclosure fence for the red foxes facing the public had a section approximately 1ft in length where the wires were
distorted and warped from previous fallen tree branch damage. There was at least one section of wire warped in a
manner that created a sharp point. Both areas pose a risk of harm through entrapment or injury from sharp points. The
outdoor housing facilities shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury and to contain the animals
from injury.
Correct by July 6th, 2026.

The enclosure for the two Bald Eagles had a 3.5 feet long by 4.0 inch wide gap between the glass window and the pipe
holding up the wire frame at the top of the enclosure. The gap created is large enough to allow other animals into the
enclosure. Wild animals can introduce pathogens and disease to the facility's flock. The primary enclosure must be
constructed and maintained so that they contain the animals securely and restrict other animals from entering the
enclosure.
Correct by June 27th, 2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
The physical environment for multiple bird species, including bald eagles, ring-neck pheasant, red-tailed hawk, golden
eagle, black vulture, great-horned owl and barred owl lacked adequate environmental enrichment. Very limited
enrichment was provided through the provision of natural perches, and no additional cage complexity, manipulable
objects or foraging and task-oriented feeding methods were observed.
A lack of adequate environmental enrichment for these species may negatively affect psychological well-being and could
result in abnormal behavior. The physical environment in the primary enclosures must be enriched by materials or
activities that would provide the birds with the means to express non-injurious species-typical activities. With the attending
veterinarian’s oversight, the facility must implement species-appropriate environmental enrichments to meet the
behavioral and psychological needs of the birds.
Correct by July 18th, 2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not follow an Environmental Enhancement plan for birds that includes special considerations for
individually housed social species of birds that are unable to see and hear birds of their own or compatible species. There
is one female Ringneck Pheasant currently singly housed and is unable to see or hear compatible birds. The facility's
current enrichment plan is limited to providing natural perches and a natural enclosure setting. Failure to follow a plan for
birds requiring special consideration may result in inadequate care in promoting and addressing their psychological well-
being. Certain birds must be provided special attention regarding enhancement of their environment in accordance with
the instructions of the attending veterinarian.
Correct by July 6th, 2026.

The current food receptable for the Ring-Necked Pheasant is not located so as to minimize any risk of contamination by
excreta and pests. The food receptacle for the pheasant is placed on the floor of their shelter, and was observed to have
at least two chipmunks consuming the pheasant's food. One chipmunk was observed standing in the food bowl. The
presence of pests around and within the bird's food source poses a risk of disease transmission and contamination. Food
and any food receptacles must be located so as to minimize any risk of contamination by excreta, precipitation, and pests.
Correct by July 6th, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the superintendent.
Additional Inspectors:
Sarah Roloff n
